targets.authors: Pennycook, G., McPhetres, J., Zhang, Y., Lu, J. G., & Rand, D. G.
targets.title: Fighting COVID-19 misinformation on social media: Experimental evidence for a scalable accuracy-nudge intervention.
targets.evidence_quote:
The
present study aims to replicate Pennycook et al. and test whether
ﬁndings from Pennycook et al. or Roozenbeek et al. are replicated in
a third U.S. sample.
targets.outcome_quote:
The accuracy nudge’s effect did not replicate in the Kyrgyzstan
sample (n = 1,049). Results were mixed in India (n = 703) and the United States (n = 829); the nudge decreased willingness to share
some misinformation but it did not signiﬁcantly increase willingness to share true information.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Aggregated across the two replication studies and three country samples; authors explicitly describe partial or mixed replication. Vaccine-specific measures extend the original claim.

targets.authors: Roozenbeek, J., Freeman, A. L. J., & van der Linden, S.
targets.title: How accurate are accuracy-nudge interventions? A preregistered direct replication of Pennycook et al. (2020).
targets.evidence_quote:
The
present study aims to replicate Pennycook et al. and test whether
ﬁndings from Pennycook et al. or Roozenbeek et al. are replicated in
a third U.S. sample.
targets.outcome_quote:
Our ﬁndings
are in partial agreement with Roozenbeek and colleagues. The
accuracy nudge did not decrease willingness to share false general
COVID-19 information in Kyrgyzstan or the United States. In India,
the accuracy nudge did decrease willingness to share general
COVID-19 misinformation. However, in full agreement with Roo-
zenbeek and colleagues, we found strong evidence suggesting
that the accuracy nudge does not signiﬁcantly increase the spread
of true information in any of the three countries.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Aggregated across the two replication studies and three country samples; authors explicitly describe partial or mixed replication. Vaccine-specific measures extend the original claim.
